intro: Grilling is the one method where most of the oil never arrives on the plate. It runs off the food, drips between the bars and burns on the coals below.
Which bottle you reach for matters less than the moment you reach for it: two pours, two oils, and only one of them tasted.

sections.heading: Oil the food, not the grate

blocks.text: Brush the oil onto the food, not onto the bars. Oil on a hot grate burns off within seconds and leaves a sticky residue that grips rather than releases. A thin film on the food is what stops sticking and browns first, and it takes far less oil.

items: **Pat the food dry first.** Oil slides off a wet surface, and water steams rather than browns.
**Brush, do not pour.** A teaspoon covers a chicken thigh.
**Clean and hot beats oiled.** Scrape the bars and heat them through.

sections.heading: Why a marinade's oil mostly drips and burns

blocks.text: Most of the oil in a marinade never reaches anybody. It runs off on the way to the grill, drips between the bars and burns on the fire below, and the little that clings sits in the hottest place in the kitchen.

That is not a case against marinating. The oil still carries garlic, chilli and herbs onto the surface, as [olive oil marinade](/blog/olive-oil-marinade-what-it-does) sets out. The question is which bottle.

sections.heading: Flare-ups, and what actually causes them

blocks.text: A flare-up is dripping fat catching fire, not an oil failing. Melting fat and loose marinade fall onto the coals, meet the flame and ignite, and the column of fire coats whatever sits above it in soot. More oil means more fuel arriving at once.

items: **Drain before it goes on.** Let each piece stop dripping first.
**Keep a cool zone.** Move food sideways off the flame, not upward.
**Trim the loose fat** on chicken skin and lamb, which is the fuel.

blocks.text: Direct heat means the food sits over the fire; indirect means beside it, lid down. Direct browns a thin cut in minutes. Indirect cooks a thick one through without burning the outside. Almost every grilling problem is a thick cut left over a direct fire.

blocks.text: Live charcoal runs hotter than any oil is at its best, so the pour that counts comes later. See [olive oil smoke point](/blog/olive-oil-smoke-point-what-heat-it-can-take).

sections.heading: The finishing pour, after the food comes off

blocks.text: The pour you actually taste happens once the food is off the fire. Oil meeting hot food away from the flame warms just enough to lift its aroma, and none of it burns off. This is where an extra virgin does what a refined oil cannot.

items: **Fish:** a spoonful over the flesh with lemon, straight off the grate.
**Lamb and beef:** after ten minutes of resting, not before.
**Vegetables:** while still hot, because that is when they drink it.

blocks.text: One tablespoon is the whole argument for keeping [Arabian Village extra virgin](/products) beside the serving dish, not in the bowl.

sections.heading: Satay and ikan bakar, the local cases

blocks.text: Satay and ikan bakar are where the rule shows itself. Satay is basted throughout, classically with a bruised lemongrass stalk dipped in oil, and that basting oil does mechanical work: keeping a thin surface from drying over a fast fire.
Ikan bakar is gentler. The fish is coated in sambal, often wrapped in banana leaf, and cooked at a distance rather than seared. Oil the fish, not the wire basket, and drizzle once it is opened.
Brush the food, never the grate. Drain before the fire, because the oil that drips is the oil that flares. Marinate with something plain and let the extra virgin land afterwards.

faqs.q: Can you use olive oil for grilling?
faqs.a: Yes, in two places: a thin film brushed onto the food before it goes on, and a drizzle after it comes off. Use a plain oil for the first and an extra virgin for the second.

faqs.q: Should I oil the grill grate or the food?
faqs.a: The food. Oil on hot bars burns off almost at once and leaves a residue that makes sticking worse. A clean, properly heated grate plus a light film on the food releases cleanly.

faqs.q: Why does my barbecue flare up when I put food on?
faqs.a: Fat and marinade dripping onto the fire are igniting. Drain each piece before it goes on, trim loose fat, and keep an unlit area to slide food across to when flames come up.

faqs.q: Does olive oil burn on the barbecue?
faqs.a: Oil sitting directly over live coals will darken and smoke, as any oil does at grill temperatures. That is why the marinade takes a cheap oil and the good oil goes on afterwards.

faqs.q: How much oil should I brush on before grilling?
faqs.a: Roughly a teaspoon per portion, enough to leave a sheen with nothing pooling. If oil runs off as you carry the food to the grill, there is too much on it.

faqs.q: Can I use extra virgin olive oil for satay?
faqs.a: Use a plain oil on the basting brush, since most of it drips into the fire. A spoonful of extra virgin over the skewers on the plate is where the difference is actually tasted.

faqs.q: Do I oil fish before grilling it?
faqs.a: Yes, and only the fish. Pat it dry, brush a thin film over the skin, then grill over a moderate rather than a fierce fire. Oiling the basket or the bars does nothing useful.
